iut_type: Pre-registration consulting (Move Corporation), electrically-identical product rebranded under a different selling company still requires a brand-new full-fee registration
customer_question: If a product is electrically completely identical (only the printed silk/labeling on the product differs) but is sold by a different company than the one already registered, is full SIG certification (paying the $11,040 fee again) really required? Couldn't this be handled more simply, like a listing with attached test results instead of a full new registration?
question_variants: Is there any reduced-cost or expedited path for registering an electrically-identical product under a new brand?
Since the product was already tested and passed once, shouldn't a second company be able to just reference that result without paying again?
actual_issue: The customer hoped that because the underlying product was electrically identical to an already-registered one (differing only in cosmetic labeling), a second selling company could register it more cheaply or simply by referencing the existing test results, rather than paying the full registration fee again.
plain_english_explanation: Bluetooth SIG specifically requires that when an already-qualified OEM/ODM product is sold under a nameplate bearing a different selling company's name than the one already registered, that new selling company must complete its own brand-new registration under its own name -- there is no reduced-cost or 'listing with attached test results' shortcut for this situation, regardless of how electrically identical the underlying product is. The free derivative Product List addition mechanism only works for adding model names within an already-registered company's own existing registration -- it cannot be used to extend one company's registration to cover a different company's branded version of the same product, since a different company has no access to add a derivative listing into another company's registration. Cosmetic differences alone (such as different silk-printed text on the product, with the selling company's nameplate name unchanged) can still be added as a free derivative within the same registration -- the distinguishing factor is specifically whether the selling company's nameplate name itself differs, not whether any cosmetic detail differs.
consultant_answer: Unfortunately no -- Bluetooth SIG requires that when an already-qualified product is sold under a different selling company's nameplate name, that new company must complete its own brand-new, full-fee registration under its own name. There's no reduced-cost or 'listing with test results attached' shortcut for this, no matter how electrically identical the product is to the already-registered version. The free derivative Product List addition only works within an already-registered company's own existing registration -- it can't be used to extend coverage to a different company's branded version, since that company has no access to add anything into another company's registration. If only cosmetic details (like silk-printed text) differ but the selling company's nameplate name itself is unchanged, that can still be added as a free derivative -- it's specifically the nameplate company name that determines this, not any other cosmetic difference.
decision_logic: Whether an electrically-identical product variant can be added as a free derivative versus requiring a brand-new full registration depends entirely on whether the selling company's nameplate name is the same as the already-registered company -- any difference in that specific identifier requires a new registration with no shortcut, regardless of how minor other cosmetic or electrical differences are (or aren't).
final_recommendation: When a customer proposes registering an electrically-identical product under a different brand name, be direct and clear that no shortcut exists -- a full, separately-paid registration is required, and clarify that the free derivative mechanism is strictly limited to additions within the same already-registered company's own registration.
risk_if_done_wrong: A customer attempting to add a different company's branded version of an identical product as a free derivative under the original registrant's account would find this impossible, since the new company has no access rights to that registration -- discovering this only after attempting it would waste time relative to learning upfront that a new registration is unavoidable.
